chapters.title: The Book and Its Author
paragraphs: Treasure Island is the most famous pirate story ever written, and the reason the modern world pictures pirates the way it does: the treasure map marked with an X, the parrot on the shoulder, the wooden leg, the rum-soaked sea song. It was written by Robert Louis Stevenson, a Scottish author born in Edinburgh in 1850, who lived much of his short life traveling in search of a climate kind to his failing lungs. He died in Samoa in 1894, at forty-four, and was buried on a hilltop there.

Stevenson first published Treasure Island as a serial for boys in a magazine in 1881, and it appeared as a book in 1883. He had begun it as a game: his stepson drew a map of an imaginary island, and Stevenson built a story around it, writing a chapter a day. The tale is told in the first person by Jim Hawkins, a boy who begins as the son of an innkeeper and is swept into a voyage across the world in search of buried treasure.

What keeps the book alive is not only the adventure but the moral fog it sails through. Its most vivid character, the ship's cook Long John Silver, is charming, funny, terrifying, and impossible to place neatly on the side of good or evil. This selection follows the spine of the novel — from the inn on the English coast to the island, the mutiny, and the treasure — condensing some passages and keeping the story's famous moments as Stevenson made them.

Stevenson wrote the book in a white heat of invention during a rainy holiday in Scotland, and he poured into it everything a boy could want: a haunted inn, a blind beggar with a tapping stick, a one-legged cook with a parrot, a treasure map, a mutiny, a desert island, and a battle in a log fort. But he also poured in something rarer — a clear-eyed sense that adventure has a cost, and that the line between the honest sailor and the pirate is thinner than we like to think.

The pirates of Treasure Island were drawn from real history. Captain Flint, though he never appears alive in the book, is named for the age of piracy's most feared captains, and the novel's details — the black spot, the marooning of sailors, the division of loot — come from true accounts of buccaneers in the Caribbean. Stevenson took those raw materials and gave them something history rarely supplies: unforgettable characters who feel alive on the page.

The story's power also comes from its narrator. Jim Hawkins is not a hero in the grand style; he is an ordinary boy who is brave when he must be, frightened when any sensible person would be, and honest about both. He makes mistakes — impulsive, dangerous mistakes — and some of them nearly get everyone killed. Readers have loved him for more than a century because he feels real: he is the reader, dropped into the adventure.

Since 1883 the book has never been out of print. It has been filmed, staged, illustrated, and imitated hundreds of times, and its inventions have become the common property of the world: when we picture a pirate today, we are picturing Long John Silver. Few books have shaped the imagination of childhood so completely, and few adventure stories repay rereading as an adult so well.

This selection keeps the novel's spine intact — every great scene in its proper order — while condensing the long passages of sailing and waiting that fill a nineteenth-century novel. Where Stevenson wrote a famous line that the world knows by heart, you will find his own words. Everywhere else, the story is told faithfully in fewer words, so that the whole voyage can be read in one long sitting.

chapters.title: The Admiral Benbow
paragraphs: Jim Hawkins was a boy when the old sailor first came to the Admiral Benbow, the inn his father kept on the lonely coast of England. The man was tall and strong, with a face browned by sun and scarred by a cutlass, his hands rough and dirty, his nails black and broken. He carried his sea chest behind him in a handbarrow, and he took a room overlooking the cove, paying for his lodging in advance with gold coins.

He was a quiet lodger but a strange one. He spent his days walking the cliffs with a brass telescope, watching the road and the sea as if he expected something — or someone. In the evenings he sat by the fire drinking rum, and when he had drunk enough he would sing an old sea song that Jim never forgot, slamming his hand on the table for the chorus: Fifteen men on the dead man's chest — Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum! The neighbors grew frightened of him, and the inn fell quiet, for no respectable traveler would stay where such a man drank and sang.

The sailor's name was Billy Bones. He hired Jim to keep a lookout for him, paying the boy a silver coin each month for a single piece of work: to watch for a seafaring man with one leg. Bones lived in terror of that man, and of his old shipmates generally. He told Jim wild stories of the pirate Captain Flint, the most bloodthirsty buccaneer that ever sailed, and of the treasure Flint had buried on a distant island — gold and silver enough to make a man rich for life.

Then one January morning a new visitor came to the inn: a pale, unremarkable man with two fingers missing from his left hand. He called himself Black Dog. He and Bones fell into talk, and the talk turned to the past, and the past turned to a quarrel, and in a moment the two men had cutlasses out and were slashing at each other across the parlor. Black Dog fled, wounded, and Bones collapsed with a stroke brought on by drink and rage.

The doctor who was called was Dr. Livesey, the local physician and magistrate, a man as brave as he was kind. He warned Bones plainly that another bout of rum would kill him, and Bones, terrified, swore off the bottle for a week — until the doctor's back was turned. Jim nursed him, and Bones, in his feverish gratitude, promised the boy a share of Flint's treasure if he would stand by him, for his old crew were hunting him, and they meant to have what he carried.

What Bones carried, though he never showed it to Jim, was the thing his old shipmates wanted: a map. For Billy Bones had been Captain Flint's mate, and when Flint died, the map of the buried treasure had come into Bones's hands. That was why Black Dog had come asking questions. That was why Bones watched the road with his telescope. The wolves were circling, and they were closing in.

Two days after the fight with Black Dog, Jim was sent on an errand, and when he returned he found his father dying and the inn in an uproar. His father died that evening, and while Jim and his mother grieved, a new terror arrived at the door: a blind beggar, tapping his way along the road with a stick. He seized Jim's hand in a grip of iron and demanded to be led to the captain — to Billy Bones.

The blind man was Pew, and he was no beggar but a pirate. Alone with Bones in the parlor, he pressed something into the sailor's hand and was gone before Jim could follow. Bones stared at what he had been given — a blackened circle of paper, the pirates' summons, the Black Spot — and the shock and the rum together stopped his heart. He fell dead on the floor, and the Black Spot fluttered from his fingers.

Jim understood at once what it meant. The crew were coming for the chest that very night. With his mother he forced the dead man's sea chest open and searched it for the thing worth dying over — the map — while Pew's gang could be heard gathering outside. They found coins, a quadrant, papers, and at the bottom, wrapped in oilcloth, a chart of an island with three red crosses and writing that named the spot where the bulk of Flint's treasure lay buried.

The Admiral Benbow stood alone on the coast road, a long, low house with a sign that creaked in the wind, and in those days it did a thin trade. Jim's father was a sick man, growing weaker through the winter, and his mother ran the inn with Jim's help. The arrival of Billy Bones, with his gold and his sea chest, should have been a blessing. Instead it cast a shadow over the house that deepened week by week.

Bones paid his way fairly, and for a time he was no worse than a rough, silent lodger. But as the weeks passed he drank more and sang louder, and his songs and stories drove custom away. Coach drivers and farmers who had stopped for ale began to pass the door by, and the inn grew emptier and poorer. Jim's father worried, and his mother said nothing, as mothers will when the rent is paid in gold.

What frightened Jim most was not the singing but the watching. Bones would climb the cliff path with his telescope and stand for hours staring at the cove and the road, and sometimes he would come down white-faced and order an extra tot of rum. Once he seized Jim's arm and made the boy swear to watch for the one-legged man, describing him over and over, as if repetition could keep the terror at bay. Jim dreamed about that missing leg.

The stories Bones told were worse than the watching. On winter evenings, with the wind howling outside, he would describe life under Captain Flint: the battles, the plundered ships, the maroonings, the treasure buried on an island no honest chart had ever shown. He spoke of Flint with a mixture of terror and admiration, and Jim drank it all in — the gold, the danger, the freedom — without understanding that he was listening to the confession of a criminal.

Then came Black Dog, and the fight, and the stroke, and Dr. Livesey's stern warning. For a week Bones lay in bed, and Jim brought him his broth, and the old pirate wept and swore he would reform. But the moment he could stand, he was at the rum again, and Jim understood with a child's sudden clarity that Billy Bones was a doomed man — not because his enemies would find him, though they would, but because he could not save himself from himself.

Looking back, Jim could see that Billy Bones had been running on borrowed time from the first day he walked into the inn. Every gold coin he paid, every song he sang, every night he spent watching the road was part of a debt coming due — the debt of a pirate's life, which is always paid in the end. The tragedy of Bones was not that his enemies found him, but that he had nowhere else to go: the sea had used him up, and the land had no place for him.

chapters.title: The Black Spot
paragraphs: Jim and his mother fled the inn with the oilcloth packet, and none too soon. Pew's men broke in moments later, ransacked the chest, and found nothing but coins — for the map was already in Jim's pocket. They quarreled among themselves in the dark, and then, out in the lane, came the thunder of horses' hooves. The revenue officers were riding down, and the pirates scattered. Blind Pew, abandoned by his own mates, was run down in the road and killed beneath the hooves, his stick clattering beside him.

Jim ran with the packet to the hall of Squire Trelawney, the great landowner of the district, where Dr. Livesey was dining. In the lamplight they opened the oilcloth together, and there it was: a map of an island, drawn in a bold hand, with latitudes and longitudes, soundings and anchorages, and three crosses in red ink marking where the treasure of Captain Flint was buried. The writing at the bottom gave the details, in Flint's own hand.

The squire, a warm-hearted, impulsive gentleman, was beside himself with delight. He declared on the spot that they would fit out a ship, hire a crew, and sail for the island to recover the treasure. Dr. Livesey, cooler and wiser, warned him of one danger: the squire could keep no secret, and if word of the map got out in Bristol, every cutthroat in England would want a share. The squire laughed the warning off — and then proved it true, for within days of reaching Bristol, half the town seemed to know about the voyage.

Still, the expedition was launched. The squire bought a fine schooner, the Hispaniola, and set about hiring officers and men. Livesey would go as ship's doctor. And it was in Bristol, while the ship was being fitted out, that the squire fell under the spell of the most persuasive man Jim had ever met — the man who would make this voyage a legend and nearly a massacre.

The looting of the chest was a desperate business. Jim's mother, brave as any sailor, insisted on taking only what Bones owed them for his lodging — not a coin more — even with Pew's gang pounding at the door. They counted out the money by the light of a single candle while the pirates' voices grew louder outside, and it was this stubborn honesty, in the middle of terror, that Jim never forgot.

They escaped by the back as the gang broke in the front, and ran for the village in the moonlight, Jim clutching the oilcloth packet, his mother stumbling beside him. Behind them they heard glass breaking and men shouting, and then the thunder of the revenue officers' horses, and Pew's dreadful scream. They hid in a ditch until it was over, and then walked the long road to the squire's hall with the map.

Dr. Livesey studied the map with a professional eye, and what he saw made even his calm face serious. Here were soundings and anchorages marked with a seaman's care, and the three red crosses, and notes in Flint's own crabbed hand giving the bearings of the treasure. It was genuine beyond doubt — the life's plunder of the most feared pirate of his age, waiting on an island in the distant seas.

The squire's excitement knew no bounds, and his indiscretion matched it. He talked of nothing but the treasure for days, and wrote letters full of it, and bustled about Bristol telling all and sundry that he was fitting out a ship for a great voyage. Livesey warned him again, and the squire promised secrecy with one breath and broke it with the next. It was this loose tongue, as much as anything, that put Flint's old crew on their trail.

Within weeks the Hispaniola was bought, fitted, and provisioned, and Jim said goodbye to his mother and the Admiral Benbow. He rode to Bristol with his heart pounding, the map sewn into his clothes, bound for the sea and the greatest adventure any boy ever had. Behind him, the little inn stood quiet on the cliff road, and ahead lay the wide water — and Long John Silver, waiting by the docks with his crutch and his smile.

Years later Jim would remember that ride to the squire's hall as the true beginning of everything: the moonlit road, his mother's hand in his, the oilcloth packet heavy as sin in his pocket. He had been an innkeeper's boy that morning; by midnight he was the bearer of a pirate's map, and his old life was over. Adventure, he learned, does not knock politely — it kicks the door in.

chapters.title: Bristol: The Voyage Begins
paragraphs: Bristol in those days was the great port of the west of England, and the squire threw himself into the preparations with money flying. He wrote to Jim and the doctor in high spirits: the Hispaniola was bought and fitted, a captain engaged, and — best of all — he had found the very man to cook for them, a one-legged seaman who kept a tavern by the docks and knew every sailor worth hiring in the port.

The captain was Smollett, a sharp, disciplined officer who did not please the squire at all, for he arrived with complaints before the anchor was even weighed. He did not like the voyage, he said; he did not like the crew, who had been picked up too easily and knew too much about their destination; and he did not like the way the treasure hunt was being talked about openly in every tavern in Bristol. The squire called him impertinent. Dr. Livesey, who judged men better, told the captain quietly that he would stand by him.

Smollett's unease was well founded. A voyage to find buried treasure was a magnet for exactly the wrong kind of sailor, and the squire, for all his generosity, had hired with a free hand and asked few questions. The crew signed on cheerfully, a rough, able-looking body of men, and among the last to come aboard was the cook the squire had praised so highly — the one-legged tavern-keeper, Long John Silver.

On the morning of sailing, the Hispaniola dropped down the Avon with a fair wind, Jim wild with excitement at his first sight of the open sea. The captain set strict discipline from the first hour: no rum aft without orders, weapons secured, watches kept sharp. Silver, for his part, was everywhere at once — laughing, working, making friends with every man aboard, and especially kind to Jim, who began to think him the best of good fellows. It was the pleasantest voyage imaginable, and that was precisely the danger.

The fitting-out of the Hispaniola was a busy, happy time for Jim, who ran errands all over the docks and stared at everything. Bristol was full of sailors — honest tars and rogues cheek by jowl — and the squire's money hired quickly. The mates were chosen: Mr. Arrow, a cheerful, easygoing fellow, and the boatswain Job Anderson, a great strong seaman. The crew that signed on looked able enough, though the captain eyed them sourly.

It was at Silver's tavern, the Spy-glass, that the squire had first met the cook, and Silver had charmed him as completely as he charmed everyone. He knew every man in Bristol worth hiring, the squire wrote, and he had picked the crew himself — a crew of hand-picked seamen, tough and experienced. The squire could not praise him enough. Dr. Livesey, reading the letter, frowned at the news that the crew had been chosen by the cook.

Silver came aboard with his sea chest and his parrot and his crutch, and from the first hour he made himself indispensable. He cooked, he joked, he sang, he knew every man's name by the second day, and he took a particular liking to Jim, calling him son and teaching him sailor's knots and sea songs. Jim, lonely for a friend his own age among rough men, gave the cook his whole heart.

Captain Smollett ran his ship with an iron hand, and the squire chafed under it, but the doctor backed the captain in everything. Discipline was strict: the crew were kept busy, rum was rationed, and the treasure — though everyone aboard seemed to know about it — was never mentioned aft. The Hispaniola proved a fine sailer, and for weeks they ran before fair winds, the island drawing nearer, and no one guessed what was brewing below decks.

There were small signs, for those with eyes to see. The first mate, Mr. Arrow, drank himself useless and vanished one dark night — fallen overboard, all agreed, though no one had seen him fall. The crew grew familiar and insolent among themselves, whispering in knots. Silver smoothed everything over with his laugh, and the squire thought him a treasure. Only the captain kept his own counsel, and cleaned his pistols, and waited.

On the last evening before they sailed, Jim stood on the deck of the Hispaniola and watched the lights of Bristol twinkle along the water. He felt the ship move under him like a living thing, and smelled tar and salt and canvas, and thought his heart would burst with happiness. If anyone had told him then what the voyage would cost — in blood, in terror, in the loss of his innocence — he would not have believed it, and perhaps he would have sailed anyway.

chapters.title: The Sea Cook
paragraphs: Long John Silver was the most remarkable man our hero had ever seen. He had lost his leg in service under a famous admiral, and he hopped about the galley on his crutch as nimbly as any two-legged man, cooking, cleaning, and singing as he worked. His face was broad and pleasant, his manner full of cheerful good humor, and he had a way of talking to a boy as if the boy were the most important person in the world. Jim loved him within a week.

Silver's constant companion was his parrot, a green bird he called Captain Flint, after his old commander. The bird was a marvel and a nuisance, screaming its few phrases at all hours in a voice like a rusty hinge. Its favorite cry, which it repeated until the whole ship knew it by heart, was the two words that would haunt Jim Hawkins for the rest of his life: Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!

But there was another side to the cook, glimpsed only in passing. Once, ashore in Bristol before they sailed, Jim had seen Silver in earnest talk with Black Dog — the very pirate who had fought Billy Bones at the inn. When Jim told Silver what he had seen, the cook laughed it off with perfect ease, swearing he had never laid eyes on the man. Jim, who had liked Silver too much to doubt him, let the matter drop. He would remember that laugh later, and understand it.

For all his charm, Silver could not charm Captain Smollett. The captain watched the cook with cold, narrow eyes, and Silver watched the captain back with a smile that never quite reached his own. Dr. Livesey, too, kept his counsel, though he admitted to Jim that Silver was a man of remarkable ability — the kind of man who might rise to anything, or sink to anything. The voyage wore on through fine weather, the island drawing nearer every day, and the crew growing restless with the thought of gold.

Silver loved to talk about his past, and his stories were the delight of the forecastle. He had sailed under the great admirals, he said, and lost his leg in honorable service — though the doctor noticed that the dates and battles shifted a little each time the tale was told. He spoke of the sea with a poet's feeling and a thief's knowledge, and Jim could have listened to him for hours.

The parrot, Captain Flint, was two hundred years old by Silver's account, and had sailed with the great pirates of the age. Whether or not that was true, the bird was a wonder: it would sit on Silver's shoulder through a whole watch, preening and muttering, and then burst without warning into its piercing scream of Pieces of eight! until the men roared with laughter. Only Jim, remembering Billy Bones, sometimes found the joke less funny than the others did.

Jim became Silver's special messenger and errand boy, proud of the cook's favor. He carried dishes, ran messages, and sat by the galley door in the evenings listening to the men's talk. It was there, half-listening and half-dreaming, that he first noticed how the crew deferred to Silver — not as a cook, but as something more. When Silver spoke, the roughest men listened. When he frowned, they fell silent.

Captain Smollett's dislike of the cook never wavered, and it puzzled Jim, who could see no fault in his friend. Once Jim asked the doctor about it, and Livesey answered thoughtfully: Silver was a man of great ability, he said, and ability without principle was the most dangerous thing in the world. Jim pondered that, watching Silver hop laughing across the deck, and could not make it fit the man he knew.

So the voyage wore on in fair weather and false friendship, and Jim's liking for Silver grew into something like love. The cook taught him to hand, reef, and steer; praised his quickness; told him he would make a fine seaman. And all the while, below that broad and smiling face, Long John Silver was counting the days to the island, and counting the honest men aboard, and deciding, one by one, which of them would live to see home again.

There was one moment, late in the voyage, that Jim never forgot. He had asked Silver, idly, what he would do with his share of the treasure, and the cook's face had changed — just for an instant — into something hard and hungry and old. Then the smile came back like the sun, and Silver laughed and said he would buy a tavern and keep parrots. Jim laughed too, uneasily, and the moment passed. But he remembered it in the apple barrel.

chapters.title: The Apple Barrel
paragraphs: It happened on the night before they expected to sight the island. Jim, restless and hungry for an apple, climbed into the great apple barrel on deck and burrowed down among the fruit — and fell asleep there, hidden below the rim. He woke to the sound of voices: men settling themselves against the barrel to talk in the dark, unaware that a boy lay listening at their feet. One of the voices was Long John Silver's.

What Jim heard froze the blood in his veins. Silver was laying out, calmly and completely, a plan for mutiny. When the treasure was found, the honest men aboard — the captain, the squire, the doctor — were to be killed. Silver spoke of his old life under Captain Flint with pride, and named the men of the crew who were Flint's old pirates, sworn to the plot. Others, he said, could be won over or dealt with. The tone was businesslike, almost cheerful, as if murder were a matter of stores and rigging.

And then Jim heard the other Silver — the one beneath the smile. When one of the men wavered, Silver's voice turned to iron, and he described what happened to sailors who crossed him, and to the crews of ships he had sailed with that never came home. Jim, trembling in the dark among the apples, understood at last what the laugh in Bristol had meant, and what the pleasant cook truly was: the most dangerous man aboard the Hispaniola, and the crew's true captain in all but name.

Jim slipped from the barrel unseen and ran to warn the captain, the squire, and the doctor. They listened in grim silence. Now Smollett's complaints made terrible sense: the crew the squire had hired so freely were Flint's old wolves, and Silver had picked them himself. The honest men aboard numbered barely half a dozen against nearly twenty pirates. From that moment, every smile on deck was a mask, and every order a move in a game whose stakes were their lives.

A council of war was held in the cabin. They could not turn back — the crew would suspect at once. They could not fight openly — they were outnumbered three to one. Their only hope was to reach the island first, get ashore with arms and powder, and hold some strong place until help or fortune favored them. The map showed an old stockade on the island, built by Flint's men years before. If they could reach it and fortify it, they might stand a siege. It was a thin hope, but it was the only one they had.

The day before they sighted the island, the whole ship was on edge. The crew had caught the gold fever badly: they sang at their work, they quarreled over nothing, and they watched the horizon with hungry eyes. Silver moved among them like a shepherd, calming one man, flattering another, keeping the peace with jokes and promises. Only in the cabin was the air cold, for the captain knew what the rest only felt.

Jim had gone to the apple barrel for the simplest of reasons — he wanted an apple — and stayed because the barrel was warm and the motion of the ship was soothing. He was half-asleep when the voices began: Silver, and young Dick Johnson, and Israel Hands the coxswain, settling down for a talk they thought was private. Jim lay still as death, afraid to breathe.

What he learned, word by word, was the whole of the plot. Silver and his men meant to wait until the treasure was aboard, then kill the captain, the squire, the doctor, and every honest man with them. Some of the crew were Flint's old pirates, sworn to Silver from the start. Others — like Dick — were being recruited one by one, tempted with gold and frightened with threats. Only a handful, Silver said, would need killing outright: the rest could be marooned, or won over.

The coldest moment came when Silver spoke of the two honest sailors, Tom and Alan, who had refused his approaches. Silver described, almost gently, how they would be dealt with — and Jim understood that the pleasant cook discussing murder over the barrel was the real Long John Silver, and the laughing friend of the galley was the mask. He pressed himself into the apples and prayed they would not look inside.

When the talk ended and the men moved away, Jim waited until the deck was quiet, then climbed out and ran aft. He told his story to the captain, the squire, and the doctor in a shaking whisper, and watched their faces change as the last piece of the puzzle fell into place. Smollett nodded grimly — it was what he had feared from Bristol. From that hour, the Hispaniola carried two crews: one open and one secret, sailing the same ship toward the same island, each planning the other's destruction.

The council in the cabin lasted until near dawn, and its decisions shaped everything that followed. They would keep up appearances: the squire would be his bluff self, the captain would give no sign of suspicion, and Jim would go on being Silver's favorite — the spy in the enemy's affection. It was agreed, too, that at the first sign of the island they would try to get ashore with arms. Jim listened, and felt very small, and very proud to be trusted.

chapters.title: Land Ho! The Island
paragraphs: Three days later the lookout cried land, and there it rose from the sea: Treasure Island, exactly as the map had drawn it — three miles long and five wide, with wooded hills, a high crag called the Spy-glass, and a marshy shore where the surf broke white. The honest men looked at it with dread, for every tree might hide a pirate, and the pirates looked at it with greed, for every foot of it might hide gold.

The strain broke into open defiance almost at once. Silver, sensing the crew's impatience, asked leave to take the men ashore for the afternoon, and the captain — playing for time — agreed. Jim, burning with curiosity and a boy's recklessness, slipped into one of the shore boats at the last moment and went with them. Silver went ashore hopping on his crutch, the parrot on his shoulder screaming its eternal cry, and the men scattered into the woods.

Jim slipped away from the party and ran into the trees — and within the hour he witnessed what Silver's discipline was worth. Two of the honest sailors who had refused the mutiny were murdered in the woods: one shot, one run through, while Silver stood by and watched, and then coolly talked the killers into patience, arguing that the treasure must come first and throats could be cut afterward. Jim, hidden in the bushes, heard it all, and his blood ran cold.

Fleeing deeper into the island, Jim stumbled upon a stranger — a wild-looking man dressed in goatskins, half-crazed with loneliness, who started at the sight of him and then fell on his knees in joy. He was Ben Gunn, and his story was a strange one. He had sailed with Flint himself, and three years before, on another voyage, his shipmates had marooned him on this island with a musket, a spade, and a pick — and sailed away and left him.

Three years alone, Ben Gunn said, and the words became his refrain, repeated with a shudder and a laugh. He had lived on goats and oysters, dreamed of rescue, and prayed — for he had turned pious in his solitude, after a fashion. But what he wanted most in the world, what he dreamed about, what he begged Jim for with tears in his eyes, was the simplest thing imaginable: a piece of cheese. Toasted, mostly, he said. He had dreamed of cheese every night for three years.

Ben Gunn knew about the treasure — he had been there when Flint buried it — and he knew something more: something that made him confident he could help Jim's party if they would take him off the island and treat him fair. He would not say what it was, only that he was rich, and that Dr. Livesey was the man to deal with. Jim promised to bring the doctor to him, and left the marooned man chewing on the hope of cheese and freedom.

The island lay exactly as the map had promised, and the sight of it worked on every man aboard like a spell. The pirates crowded the rails, pointing and arguing over landmarks, while the captain stood apart with his telescope, noting the reefs and the anchorage with a seaman's eye. The squire, for once, was silent. Even Dr. Livesey looked grave, for a chart is one thing and the place itself — green, silent, and watching — is another.

Silver asked permission to take the men ashore, thirteen of them, and the captain granted it — for refusal would have brought the mutiny on at once, and every hour of delay was precious. Jim, against all orders and all sense, slipped into the last boat, driven by a boy's curiosity and the feeling that he could not bear to be left behind. Silver saw him, and laughed, and let him come.

On the beach Silver mustered his men with the parrot on his shoulder, and for a little while they strolled like holidaymakers. Then the men wandered off into the woods in twos and threes, and Jim wandered after them — and came, through the trees, upon a scene he never forgot. Tom, one of the honest sailors, stood facing Silver, refusing his offers; and as Jim watched, hidden, Silver's men struck Tom down, and Silver himself drove his knife into the other loyal man, Alan, who lay dying in the ferns.

What froze Jim's blood was not only the killing but Silver's calm afterward. He wiped his knife, comforted the murderers, and reasoned with them like a father: patience, he said, the treasure first, and then they could cut throats to their hearts' content. It was the apple-barrel voice again — the iron beneath the smile — and Jim, sick with horror, slipped away into the forest before they could find him.

He ran until his legs gave out, deeper and deeper into the island's green heart, with the pirates' voices fading behind him. It was then, in a clearing among the trees, that he met the wild man in goatskins — and heard, for the first time, the strange refrain that would echo through the rest of the story: three years alone, three years alone, and the desperate, dreaming plea for cheese.

Alone in the forest, with the pirates' voices behind him and the unknown ahead, Jim felt the full weight of what he had done by slipping into that boat. He was a boy, unarmed, on an island full of murderers, with no way back to the ship. Fear rose in him like water in a sinking boat — and then, to his own surprise, a stubborn anger rose with it. He would not cower. He would find his friends, or find Ben Gunn again, or find something. He wiped his eyes and walked on.

chapters.title: The Stockade
paragraphs: While Jim was ashore, the honest party made its move. Under cover of a foggy morning, the captain, the squire, the doctor, and the three loyal servants — Redruth, Joyce, and Hunter — loaded a boat with powder, muskets, and provisions and rowed for the stockade, the old log fortress marked on the map. The pirates, drunk and quarreling in their camp, were slow to understand what was happening, and slower still to stop it.

The stockade stood on a cleared hilltop by a spring: a stout log house fenced with a palisade, built by Flint's men years before and still sound. The little garrison settled in, posted sentries, and waited. Jim rejoined them by swimming out to the ship and coming ashore in the confusion, and his news of Ben Gunn — and of the two murdered sailors — hardened every heart for what was coming.

It came at dawn. Silver himself approached under a flag of truce, magnificent and courteous, and offered terms: the map for their lives, the treasure split, no throats cut. Captain Smollett answered him with contempt, and Silver hopped away on his crutch, promising them a hot morning. An hour later the pirates came on through the woods, and the stockade erupted in musket fire.

The fight was short and savage. The pirates rushed the palisade and were beaten back with heavy losses, leaving their dead and wounded in the clearing. But victory cost the garrison dear: old Redruth, the squire's gamekeeper, was shot down and died that evening, faithful to the last; Joyce was killed outright; Hunter was badly wounded. The pirates retreated to their camp, and that night the defenders could hear them across the island, drinking and singing and quarreling over the rum.

The next day brought an unexpected visitor. Dr. Livesey, armed with his pistols and his medicine case, walked calmly out of the stockade and into the pirates' camp to treat their wounded — for the doctor would not let even mutineers die untended. He was gone for hours, and when he returned his face was grave. He had seen Ben Gunn, he told Jim quietly, and they had talked. Something was afoot, but the doctor would not say what — only that Jim must trust him, whatever happened.

The stockade was a relic of Flint's own time: a log house built of unhewn trunks, loopholed for muskets, standing in a clearing on a hill above a spring of fresh water. Around it ran a palisade of tall stakes, and though the gate hung loose and the roof leaked, it was a fortress to men who had nothing else. The little garrison worked all day to put it in order, and slept that night with muskets loaded at their sides.

Life in the siege settled into a grim routine: watches through the night, cooking and mending by day, and always the watching of the woods. The pirates made no second attack at first; they could be heard in their camp, drinking the ship's rum and quarreling among themselves. Silver, it seemed, was having trouble holding his wolves together now that the treasure was still in the ground and the ship's discipline was gone.

It was during these days that Dr. Livesey made his mysterious visits — first to the pirates' camp with his medicine case, then alone into the woods with his pistols. He would return silent and thoughtful, and when Jim pressed him he would only say that there were things afoot that the boy would understand in time. Jim trusted the doctor as he trusted no one else, and held his tongue.

The flag over the stockade was the Union Jack, and the men took turns to keep it flying, for it was the visible sign that honest men still held that hill. Captain Smollett, wounded in the battle, directed everything from his mattress, as cool as if he were on his own quarterdeck. The squire, who had found his courage at last, stood his watches without complaint. Even in that desperate place, discipline held.

And then came the night Jim could bear it no longer. He lay listening to the pirates singing drunkenly across the island, and thought of Ben Gunn's coracle hidden among the rocks, and of the Hispaniola riding at anchor with only two wounded pirates aboard. The plan formed in his mind complete and irresistible. He waited until the camp slept, slipped over the palisade without a word to anyone, and ran for the shore — toward the most reckless deed of his life.

On the last morning before Jim's escapade, the garrison held a quiet council of its own. Powder was running low, Hunter was dying of his wound, and the pirates, for all their drunkenness, still outnumbered them three to one. Captain Smollett, propped on his mattress, said what they all knew: they could not hold the stockade forever. Something had to change the game — though none of them guessed that the change would come from a boy, a coracle, and the dark.

chapters.title: Jim Cuts the Ship Adrift
paragraphs: That night Jim Hawkins, restless and stung by the feeling that he was useless in the siege, conceived a daring plan of his own. He had seen Ben Gunn's little coracle — a boat of goatskin stretched on a frame, hidden among the rocks. If he could take it out in the dark and cut the Hispaniola adrift from her anchorage, the pirates would lose their ship and their escape, and the tide would do the rest. He told no one. He simply slipped over the palisade and ran for the shore.

The coracle was light and swift, and the night was dark. Jim paddled out to where the Hispaniola rode at anchor, her riding lights burning, and with his knife he cut her cable. The tide took her at once, and she began to drift — but so did the coracle, and Jim found himself swept along in the current, clinging to his little boat while the great ship bore down toward him. In the darkness he managed to catch a trailing rope and haul himself aboard, dripping and exhausted, onto the deck of the drifting schooner.

On deck he found the ship in the hands of two men: Israel Hands, the coxswain, one of Flint's old pirates, wounded in the fighting and half-drunk; and O'Brien, another pirate, dead drunk and dead in earnest, lying in his own blood where Hands had left him. Hands, cunning even in his cups, proposed a bargain: he would help Jim beach the ship safely if Jim would give him food, drink, and a chance to desert. Jim, seeing no better choice, agreed — and kept his pistol ready.

They worked the ship together toward the shore, Hands giving orders from where he lay, Jim running to brace and haul. And then, at the moment of beaching, Hands showed his true colors: with a knife between his teeth he crawled along the deck toward the boy, meaning to kill him. Jim fled up the rigging, and as Hands hurled his knife — grazing Jim's shoulder — Jim fired both barrels of his pistol down at him. Israel Hands fell into the water, dead, and the Hispaniola ran gently aground on the sandy shore.

Jim had done it: the pirates' ship was lost to them, beached and helpless. But when he made his way back across the island at dawn, expecting a hero's welcome, he found the stockade silent and strange. The flag that flew over it was not the Union Jack but the black flag of the pirates. The stockade had fallen — or been surrendered — and Jim walked straight into the arms of Long John Silver and his men.

The coracle was Ben Gunn's own handiwork: a light frame covered with goatskin, so small that Jim could carry it, so tippy that he spent the first hundred yards learning not to capsize. But it floated, and it moved silently, and in the dark no watchman on the Hispaniola could have seen it. Jim paddled with his hands, his heart hammering, until the great black hull of the schooner loomed above him.

Cutting the cable was the work of a moment, but what followed nearly killed him. The ebb tide seized both ship and coracle, and the Hispaniola, swinging with the current, bore straight down on the tiny boat. Jim paddled for his life, and in the last second caught a trailing rope and was hauled up the ship's side, leaving the coracle spinning away into the dark. He lay on the deck gasping, alone on a drifting ship.

Below decks he found Israel Hands, the coxswain, lying wounded with a bottle for company, and the dead O'Brien sprawled in the scuppers where Hands had left him after their drunken quarrel. Hands was cunning and dangerous even half-conscious, and Jim knew it; but he also knew the ship must be beached before the tide carried her onto the reefs. So he made his bargain, and they sailed her together — the boy giving orders, the pirate obeying with murder in his heart.

The fight, when it came, was as quick as it was desperate. Hands, thinking Jim helpless, came crawling along the deck with a knife in his teeth, and Jim — who had kept his pistols loaded and ready, as the captain had taught him — swarmed up the rigging and fired down. Both shots told. Hands let go and fell with a splash, and Jim, sick and shaking, watched the schooner ground herself softly on the sand. He had won — alone, at fifteen, against Flint's own coxswain.

He slept that night in the beached ship with the dead man below, and woke at dawn to make his way back across the island, dreaming of the welcome he would get. Instead he found the stockade flying the black flag, and walked into Silver's hands. It was the bitterest moment of the voyage — and, though Jim could not know it, the moment when Silver's last and greatest gamble began.

In later years Jim would tell this part of the story with a shake of his head, marveling at his own folly. He had acted without orders, without a plan beyond the moment, risking his life and the whole expedition on a boy's impulse. It succeeded — wildly, brilliantly — but he knew, and the captain told him plainly afterward, that it might just as easily have ended with the Hispaniola on the rocks and Jim at the bottom of the sea. Courage, the captain said, is no substitute for discipline — though he clapped the boy on the shoulder as he said it.

chapters.title: Silver's Last Gamble
paragraphs: Jim's heart sank as the pirates seized him, but Long John Silver — to the fury of his own men — declared that the boy was under his protection and not a hair of his head was to be touched. Silver's power over the crew was cracking: they had lost the ship, lost the stockade's stores, and found nothing but defeat since landing. They wanted the map, and they wanted blood, and they were beginning to doubt their leader.

The pirates' answer was the Black Spot — the same summons that had killed Billy Bones. They presented it to Silver, deposing him as captain and demanding the map. Silver, cool as ever, laughed in their faces and produced the thing they wanted: the chart, which he had somehow obtained. It was the doctor's doing — Livesey had given Silver the map, in a bargain Jim could not yet understand, in exchange for Jim's life and for something else besides.

Silver read the map to the crew, and hope flared up among them again. The treasure was marked on the Spy-glass hill, and with the chart in hand they could march straight to it. Silver, restored to command by the promise of gold, ordered the expedition for the next morning — and warned Jim to stay close to him, for the boy's life was now the only coin Silver had left to bargain with. That night Jim lay awake listening to the parrot scream in its sleep: Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!

At dawn the treasure hunt set out: Silver hopping on his crutch at the head, Jim beside him as hostage, the pirates straggling behind with picks and shovels. They climbed the Spy-glass through the hot, humming woods, following the map's bearings — a tall tree, a notch in the rocks, ten feet east. And as they climbed, the island began to play tricks on them: from somewhere in the trees came a thin, wavering voice, singing the old song of Flint's crew, and the bravest pirates turned white with terror.

It was Ben Gunn's voice, though none of them knew it — the doctor's ally, haunting the woods to unnerve them. But the pirates pressed on, for gold is stronger than ghosts, and at last they stood on the shoulder of the hill where the map's three red crosses marked the spot. Silver gave the order, and the men fell to digging with a will, flinging up the earth in the burning sun.

The pirates' trial of Silver was a strange, savage piece of theater. They presented him with the Black Spot — a page torn from a Bible, blackened with charcoal — and declared him deposed. Silver received it with perfect composure, and then, to their astonishment, produced the treasure map and laid it before them. Where he had got it, none of them knew; that the doctor had given it to him was a secret between Silver and Livesey.

The map worked like magic on the crew. Their anger melted into greed, and Silver was captain again as if nothing had happened. He promised them the treasure by the next day, and they believed him, because they wanted to believe. Jim, watching, marveled at the man's power: deposed and condemned one hour, absolute master the next, all by the force of personality and a piece of paper.

That night Silver and Jim talked long by the fire, and for the first time Jim saw the cook without his mask. Silver was playing the most dangerous game of his life, he admitted: if the treasure failed, his men would kill him; if his old friends the honest men failed, the law would hang him. Jim was his only asset — a hostage to trade, a witness to his good behavior. Keep close to me, Silver said, and you may live to tell how it ended.

The march to the treasure was a nightmare of heat and fear. The pirates stumbled through the woods, quarreling and drinking, starting at every sound. Twice they found skeletons — Flint's murdered helpers, laid out as pointers to the treasure — and the men's nerve broke a little more each time. Then came the singing from the trees: a thin, eerie voice chanting the old pirate song, and the crew stood frozen, certain it was Flint's ghost come to guard his gold.

It was Ben Gunn, of course, hidden in the woods at the doctor's orders, doing his part in the plan. But the pirates did not know that, and even Silver — who suspected — could not calm them. They pressed on only because the gold was close now, glittering in their imaginations. And so they came, sweating and terrified, to the shoulder of the Spy-glass, where the map promised the treasure — and where the empty chest waited in the earth.

chapters.title: The Empty Cache
paragraphs: Two feet down their picks struck wood — the lid of a great chest, exactly as the map had promised. The pirates shouted with joy and tore the earth away, and Silver stood over them, his face unreadable. They pried the lid open, and a silence fell. The chest was empty. Not a coin, not a jewel — nothing but broken wood and emptiness where seven hundred thousand pounds in gold should have lain.

The fury of the pirates was terrible to see. They turned on Silver in a body, screaming that he had betrayed them, that the map was a trick, that he had known all along. Five of them rushed him with cutlasses drawn — and at that moment, from the woods on every side, came the crack of muskets. Dr. Livesey, the squire, and Ben Gunn burst from cover, firing into the mob. Two pirates fell; the rest broke and fled into the trees.

Then the truth came out, and Jim understood the doctor's long game at last. Ben Gunn — the marooned man, the cheese-dreamer — had found Flint's treasure months before, dug it up single-handed, and dragged it, coin by coin, to a cave on the far side of the island. That was the secret he had hinted at, and the reason Livesey had given Silver the now-worthless map: to keep the pirates digging at an empty hole while the real treasure sat safe in Ben Gunn's cave.

The little party made its way to the cave, and there it was: gold beyond dreaming — doubloons and guineas, bars and chains, piled in the lamplight, the whole of Captain Flint's hoard. They loaded it into the boats, working for days, and ferried it out to the beached Hispaniola, which they floated again and made ready for sea. Ben Gunn, feasting at last on real food, wept with joy — and got his cheese, toasted, in quantities that would have shamed a wedding.

Of the pirates, three were left behind on the island, begging for mercy; the rest were dead or fled. Silver, who had fought beside the honest men in the final skirmish and saved Jim's life twice over, was taken aboard in irons — but on the first night out, at a port where they stopped for water, he slipped over the side with a bag of coins and vanished into the dark. No one pursued him very hard. Perhaps, as the doctor said, they were all a little glad to be rid of him.

The moment of the empty chest is the hinge of the whole story. For months — for years — these men had dreamed of Flint's gold; they had mutinied and murdered for it; and now they stared into an empty hole in the ground. The silence lasted only seconds. Then, with a roar, they turned on Silver, and cutlasses flashed in the sun, and Jim thought they were all dead men.

The volley from the woods saved them. Livesey, the squire, Gray, and Ben Gunn had been waiting in ambush, and their muskets spoke with terrible effect. The pirates broke and ran, leaving two of their number dead on the hillside, and the treasure hunt ended in blood and flight. Silver, breathing hard, leaned on his crutch and laughed — the reckless laugh of a man who has looked death in the face once more and been spared.

Then came the explanations, and Jim's admiration for Dr. Livesey knew no bounds. The doctor had found Ben Gunn, heard his story, seen the cave of treasure, and made his plan: give Silver the useless map to keep the pirates busy, let them dig at the empty cache, and strike when they were gathered and disorganized. Every mysterious visit, every silent smile, had been part of it. The doctor had outplayed Long John Silver at his own game.

The work of loading the treasure took days. Boatload by boatload, the gold came down from the cave to the shore: doubloons from a dozen mints, guineas, bars of silver, jeweled chains — the plunder of twenty years of piracy, more wealth than any of them had ever imagined. Ben Gunn, who had guarded it alone for months, watched it go with the sad pride of a man giving up a child. They left him his cheese, at least, in heroic quantities.

Three pirates were left marooned on the island at their own request — or at least without much protest — for they feared the gallows more than solitude. Silver was brought aboard in irons, to face trial in England. But at the first port of call he was gone before morning, a bag of coins under his arm, vanished into the crowds of the waterfront. The captain wanted to pursue him; the doctor, after a moment, shook his head. Let him go, the look said. We owe him Jim's life.

chapters.title: Pieces of Eight
paragraphs: So the Hispaniola sailed for home with her treasure, and every man aboard had his share. The squire was richer than ever, the captain retired in comfort, Ben Gunn got his thousand pounds and spent it — as everyone had predicted — in a few short weeks, and came begging for work at the Hall, where they kept him as a lodge-keeper, happy and harmless to the end of his days. Jim Hawkins went home to his mother, who had kept the inn through it all, and the boy who had sailed as a cabin boy came back with a man's memories.

The treasure was divided fairly, and no one grudged any man his portion. But Jim learned, as he grew older, that gold got with blood carries a shadow with it. The honest sailors who had died — Redruth, Joyce, Hunter, the two men murdered in the woods — could not be brought back with any amount of doubloons. And Long John Silver, the charming villain who had nearly destroyed them all, had escaped justice with a bag of stolen coins, leaving behind the uncomfortable truth that the most dangerous man Jim ever met was also, in his way, the most generous.

For Silver had saved Jim's life, not once but twice, and had stood by the boy when his own crew would have cut his throat. Was he a villain or a friend? Jim never decided, and Stevenson never lets the reader decide either. That is the book's deepest treasure: its refusal to divide the world cleanly into heroes and villains. Silver remains splendid and terrible to the last — the cook with the crutch and the parrot, who could make a boy laugh in the morning and plan a murder by night.

And the parrot — Captain Flint, the green bird with its single endless cry — followed Jim home in his dreams. Long after the voyage was over, Jim would wake in the night hearing the surf booming on the shores of that distant island, and through it the sharp, remembered voice of the parrot, screaming the words that had been the chorus of the whole adventure: Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! It was the price of the treasure, and the price of the story, and Jim Hawkins never forgot it.

The voyage home was the strangest part of all, for the danger was past and the gold was aboard, yet no one sang. The men who had died could not be forgotten, and the treasure seemed to each of them a poor exchange for Redruth's loyalty, or Hunter's courage, or the two sailors murdered in the woods. Jim, standing at the rail watching the island sink below the horizon, felt older than his years.

Ben Gunn got his thousand pounds, as promised, and spent it in nineteen days — or so the story goes — and came back to the Hall asking for work. They made him lodge-keeper, and he was happy: a small cottage, a garden, and cheese whenever he wanted it. He would tell the tale of the island to anyone who would listen, growing grander with each telling, and the children of the district thought him a hero.

Gray, the honest sailor who had stood by them, got his share and rose in the world, becoming a mate and then a master, and a respectable family man. The squire and the doctor divided the rest fairly, and no one was cheated. It was, as the doctor said, the cleanest division of pirate gold ever made — though Jim sometimes wondered, in later years, whether any gold got with blood can ever be truly clean.

And what of Long John Silver? He was never heard of again — or rather, he was heard of in every waterfront tavern from Bristol to the Spanish Main, for his legend grew with the telling. Some said he was living rich in America; some said he was back at sea. Jim liked to think of him sitting in the sun somewhere, the parrot on his shoulder, telling his stories — and he liked to think, too, that Silver remembered the boy he had twice saved.

So ends the story of Treasure Island: with gold divided, villains punished or escaped, and a boy grown wise beyond his years. It is an adventure tale, and a pirate tale, and a treasure tale — but underneath it is something more. It is the story of how Jim Hawkins learned that men are not divided into good and bad like pieces on a board, but are tangled together, brave and cowardly, kind and cruel, all at once. And whenever he hears, in dreams, the surf on that distant shore and the sharp cry of the parrot — Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! — he remembers.
